band.lede: Monk who carried the wisdom of the Egyptian desert to the West.

who: John Cassian was a monk who spent years with the desert monks of Egypt and wrote down what they taught. John Chrysostom made him a deacon. At Marseilles he founded two monasteries and wrote the *Institutes* and the *Conferences*, which carried the desert's wisdom to the West. Augustine's followers attacked his teaching on grace.

roles.name: Monk
roles.line: At Bethlehem, near the cave of the Nativity

roles.name: Pupil
roles.line: Years among the monks of Egypt

numbers.chip: Years in Egypt, on a short visit
lines: He and his friend Germanus went to learn from the desert monks
Abba Joseph freed them from a rash promise to hurry back to Bethlehem
Seven years later they went back, made peace, and came again with a blessing
One for each of the 24 elders in Revelation 4

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 360, probably in **Scythia Minor**, today's Dobruja in Romania. Some scholars argued for Gaul. The only early witness, Gennadius, calls him “Scythian by race”.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In a well-off Christian family, with land near woods. A tutor gave him a classical education. He had a sister. He became a monk young, with his friend Germanus.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: About 435, at **Marseilles**. No early source gives the day or the cause.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: By tradition, in a marble tomb in the crypt of his own monastery of **St Victor** at Marseilles. His head and right hand were later kept there in reliquaries.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Cassian the Roman** in the Orthodox Church, probably because he wrote in Latin. Greek calendars often drop the John. The monks of Egypt called him **John**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint in the Orthodox Church. In the Catholic Church, a local saint at Marseilles, never formally canonised. The Episcopal Church remembers him.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In the East, an old monk with a grey pointed beard, sometimes hooded. In the West, from the 10th century, an author at his writing.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Three works, all in Latin: the **Institutes** (12 books), the **Conferences** (24) and **On the Incarnation**, against Nestorius (7 books).

portrait.alt: A small gold medallion from a Greek manuscript: Cassian as an old monk in a pointed dark hood, with a white beard
portrait.credit: Saint John Cassian, miniature in the Sacra Parallela of John of Damascus, 9th century. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Unknown Byzantine illuminator
portrait.caption: A medallion of Abba Cassian in the Sacra Parallela, a Greek manuscript of the 9th century. Bibliothèque nationale de France. Public domain.

west.text: **Catholic**, as a local feast of **Marseilles**. The *Roman Martyrology* of 2004 lists him this day. He is not in the General Roman Calendar, nor in the 1916 Martyrology. Also the **Episcopal Church**, as a monastic and theologian.

east.text: **Greek** churches, the **OCA** and the **Romanian** Church, in years with no 29 February.
The same churches, in leap years. In the printed service books he is the only saint with a service that day.
**Russian Church**. It keeps him on 29 February, or the 28th, by the old calendar. On today's calendar that is always 13 March.

feasts.note: Why a leap day? The oldest Greek lists, copied in Palestine in 1050 and 1063, put him on 28 February. From the 12th century a Jerusalem service book moved him to the 29th, and the printed service books kept it. 23 July is the feast of his own city, Marseilles. The Church of England and the Lutheran churches do not keep him.

traits.title: honest about his temper
traits.text: Living alone as a hermit, he still lost his temper. He was cross with his pen for being too large or too small, and with his blunt penknife. When he was hurrying to the reading, he was cross with his flint for being slow to spark. He cursed them, he admits, “or at least the devil”. His lesson: the faults you carry into the desert come with you.

traits.title: bookish, and it bothered him
traits.text: He told Abba Nesteros that the poems of his schooldays came back to him even at prayer. As he sang the Psalms, “the images of heroes fighting” rose before his eyes. Nesteros told him to give Scripture the same zeal, since “the mind of man cannot be emptied of all thoughts”.

traits.title: a friend for life
traits.text: Germanus was with him from his first days as a monk: at Bethlehem, in the desert, at Constantinople and in Rome. People said of them that “a single heart and soul existed in our two bodies”.

traits.title: gave the credit away
traits.text: He ends one of his books by telling readers where its good parts came from: “whatever in it pleases them belongs to the fathers, and whatever they dislike is all our own”.

said.lede: The oldest account of his life is one paragraph long. Gennadius, a priest of his own city, wrote it in the late 400s.

quotes.q: He wrote from experience, and in forcible language, or to speak more clearly, with meaning back of his words, and action back of his talk.
Germanus, a priest, and with him Cassianus, a deacon, of John's party, both discreet men
quotes.who: Palladius, a bishop and friend of Chrysostom, on the two envoys who reached Rome in 404 or 405

cite.text: Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom, chapter 3

quotes.q: …the first to introduce the rules of Eastern monasticism into the West

quotes.who: Cassiodorus, to his monks, about 550. In English, *read diligently, listen often* (our translation). He also warned them to read Cassian with care on free will.

cite.text: Institutions, Book 1, chapter 29, as Gibson quotes it

moments.title: A famous abbot in their cell
moments.text: Cassian and Germanus became monks at Bethlehem. One day an old man arrived as a new novice and was put in their cell. He was Pinufius, a famous abbot from Egypt, on the run from praise. He had hidden once before, working in a monastery garden for nearly three years. At Bethlehem he was found out again and taken home in honour.

moments.title: Fasts broken for guests
moments.text: In Palestine they had learned never to eat before the set hour. In Egypt the old monks broke their fast to eat with them wherever they went. Only Wednesdays and Fridays were kept. One elder explained: “The opportunity for fasting is always with me. But as I am going to conduct you on your way, I cannot always keep you with me.” To welcome them, he said, was to welcome Christ.

moments.title: A cell given away twice
moments.text: At Diolcos they longed to stay among the hermits. Abba Archebius pretended he was leaving and gave them his cell with everything in it. Then he came back and built himself another. When more monks came, he did it again, and built a third. Cassian calls it his “pious fraud”.

moments.title: Caught asleep
moments.text: Late one night old Abba Theodore walked into young Cassian's cell to see what he was doing. He found him lying down on his mat after the evening prayers. He sighed, and called him by name: “How many, O John, are at this hour communing with God, and embracing Him, and detaining Him with them, while you are deprived of so great light, enfeebled as you are with lazy sleep!”

moments.title: The broken promise
moments.text: They had promised their elders at Bethlehem, in the cave of the Nativity, to come back soon. In Egypt they told Abba Joseph they had “passed a sleepless night” over it. Joseph taught them that a rash promise may be broken for something better. They stayed seven years. Then they went home, made peace with their elders, and came back to the desert with their blessing.

moments.title: A fall they saw
moments.text: Old Heron had lived fifty years in the desert. He would not break his fast even at Easter. At last he obeyed a voice he took for an angel's, and threw himself down a well at night to prove his holiness. He died on the third day, still sure he was right. Abba Moses used it to teach them discretion: “remember what you lately saw happen before your very eyes”.

moments.title: Serapion's tears
moments.text: The bishop of Alexandria sent round a letter teaching that God has no body. Most of Egypt's monks were furious. Old Serapion had always pictured God in human form. A learned visitor persuaded him from Scripture, and everyone stood to give thanks. But in the prayer Serapion burst into tears and threw himself on the ground: “They have taken away my God from me, and I have now none to lay hold of; and whom to worship and address I know not.” Cassian was there.

moments.title: Chrysostom's deacon
moments.text: From Egypt they went to Constantinople. There the bishop, John Chrysostom, made Cassian a deacon. In 404 his enemies drove Chrysostom out. The church's gold, silver and clothing were handed to the city's officials, who signed as witnesses. Cassian and Germanus carried the receipt, to clear their bishop of the charges against him.

cite.text: On the Incarnation, Book 7, chapter 31; Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 3

moments.title: The appeal to the Pope
moments.text: The two carried a letter from Chrysostom's clergy to Pope Innocent I. His reply to Constantinople names them: “From the letters of your love that you forwarded to me through Germanus, the presbyter, and Cassianus, the deacon, I have learned, with anxious solicitude, the scenes of evil which you have placed before our eyes.” The appeal failed. Chrysostom died in exile in 407.

moments.title: Two monasteries
moments.text: Nothing is known of him for about ten years. Then he is at Marseilles. He founded a monastery for men by the tomb of the martyr Victor, and one for women. Gennadius says both were still standing in his own day.

moments.title: The two great books
moments.text: Bishop Castor of Apt wanted his new monastery run the Egyptian way, so Cassian wrote the *Institutes* for him. They cover a monk's outward life, then the eight chief faults. The *Conferences* followed: the desert abbots' talks on the inner life. Castor died before they were done. Cassian dedicated them to bishops and monks of Provence, among them Honoratus and Eucherius of Lérins.

moments.title: A last book, for Leo
moments.text: He meant to stop writing. “I had contemplated and almost determined on taking refuge in silence”, he says. But Leo, the archdeacon of Rome, asked him to answer Nestorius. Leo later became Pope Leo the Great. Nestorius, the bishop of Constantinople, would not call Mary the Mother of God. He wrote seven books in haste, before the Council of Ephesus.

moments.title: Attacked, and silent
moments.text: Prosper of Aquitaine, a lay champion of Augustine, wrote a book against his thirteenth Conference. Prosper never named him, and spoke of him with respect. No reply by Cassian is known. It is the last we hear of him.

words.note: Much of the *Conferences* is spoken by the abbots he met, and no one can say how much is theirs and how much his. The *Institutes* and *On the Incarnation* are in his own voice. Each line says whose it is. The translation is Edgar Gibson's, of 1894.

feature.kicker: A saying he could not keep
feature.q: A monk ought by all means to fly from women and bishops.
feature.ctx: An old saying of the fathers, from his book on vainglory. Neither, he explains, will let a monk keep “the quiet of his cell”. He owns that he failed on both counts, “since I could not avoid my own sister, nor escape the hands of the bishop”. The bishop's hands mean ordination: John Chrysostom made him a deacon, and he was later a priest. In Latin, {la|omnimodis monachum fugere debere mulieres et episcopos}.

quotes.q: The end of our profession indeed, as I said, is the kingdom of God or the kingdom of heaven: but the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart.
quotes.who: Abba Moses, in the first Conference: the goal a monk steers by.

quotes.q: Discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator.
quotes.who: Abba Moses, on the gift that keeps every other in balance.

quotes.q: For a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered.
quotes.who: Abba Moses, on telling your thoughts to a wise elder.

quotes.q: O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me.
quotes.who: The one-line prayer Abba Isaac gave them, to be turned over in the heart without ceasing. It is the opening of Psalm 70.

quotes.q: That is not a perfect prayer, wherein a monk understands himself and the words which he prays.
quotes.who: Abba Isaac, passing on a saying of St Antony.

myths.truth: The word is modern. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says “the word was coined between 1590 and 1600”. In his day his critics spoke of “relics of the Pelagians”. He opposed Pelagius himself, and says a Pelagian monk named Leporius “was admonished by us and corrected by God”. What is fair to say: his thirteenth Conference teaches that a good will can sometimes start in us, and the Council of Orange rejected that view in 529.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, “Semipelagianism”; On the Incarnation, Book 1, chapter 4

myths.claim: He mocked Augustine as a Cicero.
myths.truth: He names no one. His real words say the old fathers did not receive the faith “through dialectical syllogisms or the eloquence of a Cicero”. Some read the chapter as aimed at Augustine's school. The note that Cicero means Augustine was added in a modern retelling, the OCA's.

myths.claim: *The letter teaches what happened; allegory, what to believe; the moral sense, what to do; anagogy, where you are heading.* This rhyme is his.
myths.truth: A rhyme of the medieval Scholastics. His own passage is Abba Nesteros reading “one and the same Jerusalem” four ways: as the city of the Jews, the Church of Christ, the heavenly city of God, and the soul.

cite.text: Conferences, Conference 14, chapter 8; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Biblical Exegesis”

myths.claim: God gives him a feast only every fourth year, because he would not help a peasant.
myths.truth: A Russian folk tale, not church teaching. In it Cassian will not help a peasant pull his load, so as not to reach heaven with dirty clothes. St Nicholas helps and arrives dirty. So God gives Nicholas two feasts a year and Cassian one every four. On his day, Russian peasants often stayed at home for fear of his evil eye. The real date comes from old Greek calendars.

cite.text: First Things, 2013, retelling Linda Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief

myths.claim: He ruled 5,000 monks at St Victor.
myths.truth: An 11th-century claim from the abbey's own charters, made when it was stressing how old it was. Gennadius, writing in the late 400s, says only that he founded two monasteries.

stood.lede: One line is his own, from the *Institutes*. The other three are spoken by desert abbots in his *Conferences*. His translator Gibson says he made Abba Joseph's view on lying his own.

lie.work: Conferences, Conference 17, chapter 19, where Abba Joseph speaks

body.work: Conferences, Conference 2, chapter 16, where Abba Moses speaks

deeper.work: Conferences, Conference 14, chapter 11, where Abba Nesteros speaks

circle.name: Germanus
circle.text: His closest friend, some years older, from his first days as a monk. They went everywhere together, as far as Rome. Abba Joseph asked if they were brothers by birth. No, Cassian says: they were joined “in a tie of spiritual and not carnal brotherhood”. After Rome, Germanus is not heard of again. The Romanian Church made him a saint in 1992 and keeps his day with Cassian's.

cite.text: Conferences, Conference 16, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia; Orthodox Encyclopedia

circle.name: His sister
circle.text: He never names her, and admits he could not keep away from her. Scholars think she may have joined his women's house at Marseilles, but no early source says so.

circle.name: John Chrysostom
circle.text: The bishop of Constantinople, who made him a deacon. More than twenty-five years after Chrysostom's exile, Cassian still called him “a marvel of faith and purity”, and his own teacher: “for it was he who taught me what I have written”.

circle.name: Pinufius
circle.text: The famous abbot who hid as a novice in their cell at Bethlehem. When they reached Egypt, he gave them a lodging in his own cell, at the far corner of his garden.

circle.name: Abba Moses, Abba Isaac and the others
circle.text: The desert elders whose talks fill the *Conferences*. Fifteen are named.

circle.name: Leo the Great
circle.text: As archdeacon of Rome he asked Cassian to write against Nestorius. Cassian calls him “my esteemed and highly regarded friend”. He became Pope Leo the Great.

circle.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
circle.text: A lay follower of Augustine, and his first critic. Gennadius, who took Cassian's side, describes Prosper's book as “an anonymous book against certain works of Cassianus, which the church of God finds salutary, but which he brands as injurious”.

cite.text: Gennadius, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 85

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: The thirteenth Conference answered Augustine's teaching on grace, and Augustine's followers attacked it. Yet against Nestorius, Cassian still cites “Augustine the priest of Hippo Regiensis” among his witnesses.

circle.name: Nestorius
circle.text: The bishop of Constantinople he answered in seven books. He calls him “you most wicked and shameless contaminator of an illustrious city”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* thought the book written in haste, and weaker than his others.

death.big: No one recorded how he died. Gennadius says only that with his book against Nestorius he “made an end, both of writing and living, at Marseilles”.
paras: That was about 435, in the reign of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian. By tradition he was buried in the crypt of his own monastery of St Victor.

later.title: Later
later.text: Pope Urban V, who had once been abbot of St Victor, had Saint Cassian engraved on the silver casket that held his head. Many of the abbey's relics were destroyed in the Revolution, in 1794, but his head survived. In 2002 the Archbishop of Marseilles brought it to Romania for a time, where many honour him as a son of the Dobruja.

saint.big: Yes in the East, and locally in the West. The Orthodox Church counts him a saint. The Catholic Church never formally canonised him, but he is a saint of Marseilles.

churches.note: Episcopal Church, 23 July. Not in the Church of England's calendar
Not in the Missouri Synod or ELCA calendars

paras: Marseilles honoured him early. In 596 Pope Gregory the Great wrote to the abbess of the women's house he had founded, and spoke of “the day of the Saint's anniversary” there.

Then his teaching on grace counted against him. The *Roman Martyrology* left him out for centuries, and the 1916 edition still has no entry for him. In 1894 his translator Gibson wrote that his name “is not found in the Calendars of the West”. He was usually called “the blessed Cassian”.

That has changed. The *Roman Martyrology* of 2004 lists him as a saint on 23 July. An asterisk marks the entry as a local feast, read only where he is honoured. In our translation from the Latin: *At Marseilles in Provence, Saint John Cassian, priest. He founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women. Skilled by long experience of monastic life, he wrote the Institutes and the Conferences of the Fathers, to build up monks.*

quotes.q: …the monastery consecrated to the honour of Saint Cassian…
quotes.who: Pope Gregory the Great, to Respecta, abbess at Marseilles, in 596

quotes.q: Although never formally canonized, St. Gregory the Great regarded him as a saint…

prayer.intro: He ended his last book with a prayer to God, in his own voice. Here it is whole, in Gibson's translation of 1894.
prayer.q: Beyond and above all I pray with all my heart and voice, to Thee, O God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that Thou wouldest fill with the gift of Thy love whatever we have written by Thy bounteous grace. And because, as the Lord our God Thine Only Begotten Son Himself taught us, Thou hast so loved this world as to send Thine Only Begotten Son to save the world, grant to Thy people whom Thou hast redeemed that in the Incarnation of Thine Only Begotten Son they may perceive both Thy gift and His love: and that all may understand the truth that for us Thine Only Begotten, our Lord God, was born and suffered and rose again, and may so love it that the condescension of His glory may increase our love: and let not His Humility lead to a diminution of His honour in the hearts of all men, but let it ever produce an increase of love: and may we all rightly and wisely comprehend the blessings of His Sacred Compassion, so as to see that we owe the more to God, in proportion as for our sakes God humbled Himself yet lower.

reads.text: Twelve short books: a monk's day, then the eight chief faults one by one. Book 10, on restlessness, reads as if written today.

extras.title: Wonders he wrote down
extras.lede: His own books and Gennadius record no miracle of his. He wrote down wonders the desert monks told him, and his teachers put them firmly in second place.

items.title: A dead man answers
items.text: A heretic was leading the simple people of Egypt astray with clever arguments. Abba Macarius, the first monk of Scete, challenged him to raise a dead man instead. The heretic agreed, then fled Egypt. So Macarius took the people to the tombs, where the Egyptians kept their embalmed dead, and spoke to a very old body. It rose and answered him. It said it had lived under ancient kings and never heard the name of Christ. Abba Nesteros told them this. Macarius sent the man back to his rest:
items.quote: Sleep in peace with the others in your own order, to be roused again by Christ in the end.

items.title: The stolen biscuit
items.text: Abba Moses told them a story Abba Serapion used to tell the younger monks. As a boy, Serapion hid a biscuit in his clothes every day after supper, and ate it in secret. One evening his abbot, Theonas, spoke to visitors about secret thoughts. The boy broke down, laid the biscuit out before them all and begged forgiveness. Theonas told him his confession had set him free. Serapion never felt the craving again. This, he said, is what happened next:
items.quote: A burning lamp proceeding from the folds of my dress filled the cell with a sulphureous smell so that the pungency of the odour scarcely allowed us to stay there

items.title: The greater miracle
items.text: Nesteros told them the fathers never went looking for such powers. When they had them, “they would never use them, unless perhaps extreme and unavoidable necessity drove them to do so”. Macarius, he said, acted out of love, not for glory. And holiness is the greater wonder:
items.quote: It is a greater miracle to root out from one's own flesh the incentives to wantonness than to cast out unclean spirits from the bodies of others, and it is a grander sign to restrain the fierce passions of anger by the virtue of patience than to command the powers of the air.

extras.title: The eight faults
extras.lede: Eight of his twelve *Institutes* take one fault each: gluttony, fornication, love of money, anger, dejection, acedia, vainglory and pride. He calls them “the eight principal faults”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* calls them “the principal or deadly sins”.

items.title: Anger
items.text: He allows no anger at all, not even for a good reason. The words “without a cause” in Matthew 5:22, he says, were added by copyists “who did not think that anger for just causes was to be banished”. Any anger blinds:
items.quote: It makes no difference whether gold plates, or lead, or what metal you please, are placed over our eyelids, the value of the metal makes no difference in our blindness.

items.title: Acedia
items.text: Acedia is a weariness of heart that strikes a monk about noon. Some elders, he says, called it “the midday demon spoken of in the ninetieth Psalm”. That is Psalm 91 in most Bibles today. His picture of the restless monk could have been written today. The cure he passes on from Egypt is work: “a monk who works is attacked by but one devil; but an idler is tormented by countless spirits”.
items.quote: He looks about anxiously this way and that, and sighs that none of the brethren come to see him, and often goes in and out of his cell, and frequently gazes up at the sun, as if it was too slow in setting

items.title: Vainglory
items.text: Other faults weaken when beaten, he says. This one “when it is beaten rises again keener than ever for the struggle”. The elders compared it to an onion: strip off one skin and there is another. If the devil cannot make a monk vain of neat clothes, he makes him vain of shabby ones:
items.quote: For where the devil cannot create vainglory in a man by means of his well-fitting and neat dress, he tries to introduce it by means of a dirty, cheap, and uncared-for style.

extras.title: The hard parts
extras.lede: Some of his teaching troubled readers from the start, and some is hard to read today. Here it is plainly, in his words and in his critics'.

items.title: Grace and effort
items.text: In the thirteenth Conference, Abba Chaeremon teaches that God's grace comes first and does most. But sometimes, he says, the first stir of a good will is our own, and God then strengthens it. Augustine's followers heard Pelagius in this. The Council of Orange rejected the view in 529. A sixth-century list credited to Pope Gelasius called his work apocryphal, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.
items.quote: And when He sees in us some beginnings of a good will, He at once enlightens it and strengthens it and urges it on towards salvation, increasing that which He Himself implanted or which He sees to have arisen from our own efforts.

items.title: Guilty, with a plea for mercy
items.text: The *Catholic Encyclopedia* sums up the quarrel: “St. Augustine regarded man in his natural state as dead, Pelagius as quite sound, Cassian as sick.” Its judgment is that he made a purely natural act “the first step to salvation”. Gibson, his translator, was an Anglican scholar. He returns “a verdict of guilty”, with a plea for mercy. He calls Cassian's teaching “an honest attempt to vindicate human responsibility”, and says Augustine's “was one-sided and required to be balanced”. The Eastern Church, Gibson notes, always held “a milder view of the effect of the Fall”.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, “John Cassian”; Gibson, Prolegomena, chapter 1

items.title: A lie like a strong medicine
items.text: Abba Joseph teaches that a lie may be right in grave danger. Gibson says Cassian “makes his own the sentiments of Abbot Joseph on the permissibility of lying”. Augustine held that every lie is a sin. Hellebore, in Joseph's picture, is a poisonous plant used as a drug:
items.quote: And so we ought to regard a lie and to employ it as if its nature were that of hellebore; which is useful if taken when some deadly disease is threatening, but if taken without being required by some great danger is the cause of immediate death.

items.title: The father and the river
items.text: He tells this story as praise. Patermucius entered a monastery with his son of about eight. To test the father, the boy was neglected and beaten in front of him. Then the abbot told him to throw the child in the river. He threw him in, and monks posted on the bank snatched the boy out. It was revealed, Cassian says, that the father “had copied the deed of the patriarch Abraham”.
items.quote: Then he, as if this had been commanded him by the Lord, at once snatched up the child as quickly as possible, and carried him in his arms to the river's bank to throw him in.

items.title: A wife left behind
items.text: He tells how Abba Theonas left his wife, who would not agree, to become a monk. Then he insists he is only reporting what happened:
items.quote: But let no one imagine that we have invented this for the sake of encouraging divorce, as we not only in no way condemn marriage…

items.text: John Cassian, On the Incarnation of the Lord

tidbits.text: The seven deadly sins were once eight. Cassian was one of the early writers who counted eight. The number seven comes from Gregory the Great, and the great teachers of the Middle Ages kept it.

A century later, Benedict's *Rule* named the *Conferences* first among the books to read aloud to monks each evening, before the last prayers of the day. The *Rule* also opens most of its hours of prayer with the verse Abba Isaac taught him, the start of Psalm 70.

tidbits.text: Early in his desert years, restlessness drove him out of his cell to visit Abba Paul. Abba Moses told him he had not escaped it. He had given in to it, and it would attack him harder next time.
